extracted.intended_audience: poets, students of literature, and scholars studying poetic theory/creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and judging poetic diction, metre, and plot-unity in epic and tragic (dramatic and narrative) poetry, including use of metaphor, word-formation, and appropriate measure. Emphasises unity of action for drama and scale/measure/diction choices for epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (plot unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot should be constructed on dramatic principles: a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end; it should resemble a living organism in its unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For narrative imitation in a single metre the subject must be a single action (not a long sequence of loosely connected events). Epic poets may detach portions as episodes, but each tragedy (or single narrative unit) should avoid being over-vast or over-complicated; choose a portion that can be embraced in a single view. Avoid treating an entire vast war as a single, unified action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scale for epic vs tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry differs from Tragedy in scale: the beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view; epic can be larger but should still be limited so it can be apprehended as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic has capacity to include many simultaneous events and episodes (which add mass and dignity) but should not be so vast as to lack unity; tragedies should confine to the action on the stage and the part taken by the players.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts required in epic and tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Both epic and tragedy require similar structural parts (with the exception of song and spectacle): reversals (peripeteia), recognitions (anagnorisis), and scenes of suffering (pathos) as appropriate to the type (simple/complex/ethical/pathetic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, ensure the presence (or purposeful omission) of reversals and recognitions depending on whether the poem is simple or complex; thoughts and diction must be artistic. Use episodes in epic to diversify and avoid satiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and metre suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a metre appropriate to the form: heroic (epic) metre is stately and most fitting for large-scale narrative; iambic and trochaic tetrameters are stirring and suited to different kinds of verse (iambic for action/familiar speech, trochaic akin to dancing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mix different metres (mixing metres is absurd). Heroic metre readily admits rare words and metaphors; iambic should reproduce familiar speech, so favor words common to prose. Nature (experience/tradition) teaches the proper measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction perfection: 'clear without being mean'
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean; clarity comes from current/proper words but an exclusively plain diction is mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mixture is necessary: current/proper words bring perspicuity, while rare/ornamental/metaphorical words raise diction above the commonplace. Aim for perspicuity coupled with distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced use of rare/strange/ornamental/newly-coined words
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may be current, strange, metaphorical, ornamental, newly-coined, lengthened, contracted, or altered; a judicious infusion of these raises style while current words ensure clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive use of rare/strange words turns diction into jargon; excessive metaphorical language creates riddles. Use rare or ornamental forms to give distinction but not so frequently as to obscure meaning. Critics who censure exceptional word-formation (lengthening/alteration) may be mistaken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and proper use of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the application of an alien name by transference (genus→species, species→genus, species→species, or by analogy/proportion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor is powerful for raising diction and should be used with propriety; it is the mark of genius (requires an eye for resemblances). Types include proportion-based metaphors (analogy) and qualified metaphors (adding the term to which the proper word is relative). Appropriate to certain meters/genres (metaphors especially apt to iambic, serviceable in heroic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in the use of stylistic licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthening, contraction, alteration, metaphors, and rare words must be used in moderation; obtrusive employment is grotesque or ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse produces grotesque effects or makes diction ludicrous. Subtle, intermittent use (e.g., one rarer word in a line) can improve beauty; excessive deviation from idiom risks caricature or unintelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of word-formation (lengthening/contracting/altering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthening (vowel exchange or insertion), contraction (removal of parts), and alteration (partial recasting) yield distinction while maintaining partial conformity with usage for perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These licenses contribute to diction's clearness remote from commonness. They should be applied exceptionaly to gain distinction without sacrificing understandability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety in compound and unusual phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words, unusual phrases, and rare constructions give distinction but must be proper to the context and not violate the current idiom without purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe propriety in employing such expressions; critics may misunderstand their function. Such forms are often appropriate to particular genres (compound words to dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-specific diction mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Different word-kinds best suit different genres: compound words fit dithyrambs, rare words fit heroic poetry, metaphors fit iambic verse; heroic poetry can use all varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction to the genre and metre: iambic verse should use words common even in prose (current/proper, metaphorical, ornamental). In heroic/epic contexts, the stately metre allows more frequent use of rare and metaphorical language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator's presence: minimal authorial intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet (narrator) should speak as little as possible in his own person; the imitator's role is to represent action, not to intrude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive authorial intrusion detracts from imitation; let characters and action carry the poem unless minimal poetial commentary is artfully necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes in epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes (detached portions from the general story) may be admitted in epic to diversify the poem and add dignity, provided they are relevant and do not destroy unity of the subject chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use episodes to vary incident and relieve monotony; ensure each episode contributes to the subject's unity or enriches without causing confusion or undue complication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of mixing incompatible structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid composing a single large-scale poem by mixing incompatible kinds (e.g., multiple metres or attempting to cover an entire vast war as single action); keep the subject within manageable bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a segment of a larger material if necessary (as Homer does), or limit scope to what can be viewed as a unity. Mixing metres (or wholesale genre-mismatch) is incongruous and undermines effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence and phrase unity at micro-level
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence or phrase is a composite significant sound whose unity may arise from signifying one thing or from linked parts; some groups dispense with verbs yet still form unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the micro-level, craft sentences/phrases that form unities either by expressing a single idea or by coherent linkage. Attention to inflexion and temporal marking (verbs) is essential for clear expression of action and relation.
